summary: This unit teaches you to undertake compliance audits: to understand compliance, obligations and the principles of auditing; to plan a risk-based audit with objectives, scope, criteria and a checklist; to gather and record evidence by documents, observation and interviews; to grade findings and work out compliance rates; to find root causes; to report and hold the closing meeting; and to follow up corrective actions and keep the business compliant.

blocks.p: A compliance audit checks whether an organisation is doing what the laws, licences, standards and its own policies require, and gives management the evidence to fix what is wrong. This unit teaches you to plan an audit, gather and record evidence, grade findings, write a fair report, hold the closing meeting, and make sure that corrective actions really work. It is for managers, compliance and quality officers, supervisors and internal auditors in Jamaican businesses, hotels, schools and public bodies.

blocks.h: What you must be able to do

head: Task
What it means in practice
rows: Explain obligations, types of audit and the principles auditors follow
Assess risk, set objectives, scope and criteria, write the plan, arrange resources and dates
Build checklists from the criteria and decide how to sample
Examine records, observe work and interview staff, and record it in working papers
Decide major, minor or opportunity for improvement, and work out compliance rates
Use techniques such as the five whys to reach the root cause
Hold the closing meeting and write a clear, factual report with evidence
Agree corrective actions, check that they work, escalate when needed and review the programme

blocks.note: Compliance auditing is about facts and fairness. The auditor does not blame people; she compares what is done with what is required, using evidence that another person could check.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: **Compliance** means meeting the requirements that apply to the organisation: laws and regulations, licence and permit conditions, contracts, industry or national standards, and the organisation's own policies and procedures. A **compliance audit** is a planned, independent and documented check of whether practice meets those requirements. Its purpose is to find gaps early, before an inspector, an accident or a complaint finds them.
Before planning audits, the compliance manager lists every law, licence, permit and standard the business must meet. This list is the **compliance register**. For each entry record:

ul: the requirement and where it comes from (law, licence condition, contract, policy);
who in the organisation owns it;
the evidence that shows compliance (a certificate, a log, a record);
the date it expires or must be renewed or reported;
when it was last audited.

blocks.p: The register is used to set audit criteria and to choose which areas to audit.

head: Type
Who does it
Typical use
rows: The organisation's own trained staff, independent of the area audited
Regular checks of the business's own compliance
An outside firm or the regulator

blocks.p: The main difference between internal and external audits is whether the auditors **work for the organisation or not**. A medium-sized business with 150 staff might train a small team of internal auditors for regular audits and use an outside firm for specialist areas or for checks needing complete independence.

head: Principle
What it means
rows: No personal interest in, or responsibility for, the area audited; findings based on evidence, not opinion
Conclusions rest on evidence that can be checked
Information found is used only for the audit and kept private
Report truthfully, including good practice and disagreements
Spend effort where the risk of non-compliance and its impact are greatest

head: Role
Duties
rows: Senior person who commissions the audit and receives the report
Plans, leads the team, runs the meetings and writes the report
The area, manager and staff being audited; provides access and information

blocks.note: In Jamaica, compliance duties include those from regulators such as the tax authority, the Ministry of Health and Wellness (food handler permits and sanitation), the fire brigade, the environment agency and the Information Commissioner (data protection). Always check current requirements with the regulator or your legal adviser.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: A business cannot audit everything every year. Build a yearly **audit programme** that audits the **highest-risk areas first** and more often. Score each compliance area for the **likelihood** of non-compliance and the **impact** if it happens, each on a scale of 1 to 5. **Risk score = likelihood × impact**.

Factors that raise risk: severe legal penalties or harm to people, past findings, new rules, changes in staff or equipment, a complaint or incident, and areas not audited for a long time. The programme is reviewed when risks change.

head: Term
Meaning
Example
rows: What the audit is to find out
To judge whether fire safety at the Kingston warehouse meets the licence and the company's procedures
The areas, sites, activities and period covered
The Kingston warehouse, all fire safety equipment and drills, January to June
The rules and standards the work is checked against
Fire certificate conditions, the fire safety law's purpose, the company's fire procedure

blocks.note: A weak scope such as 'check safety' cannot be audited. A good scope names the place, the activities and the period.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: The plan is a short document that sets out: **objectives, scope, criteria, schedule, team, methods (documents, observation, interviews), sampling approach, resources and reporting**. Send it to the sponsor and the auditee so that the right people and records are available on the day. Agree the dates with the manager of the area being audited.

flow: Choose the area from the risk-based programme
Pick the audit team (independent and competent)
Review earlier reports, the register and the procedures
Write the plan and the checklist
Agree dates and send the plan

blocks.p: The best person to audit the payroll department's compliance with the leave policy is a **trained auditor from outside the payroll department**. People should not audit their own work. Declare any interest, such as a relative, a former role, or a friendship, and step aside from that audit.

Most audits are announced, so that people and records are ready. **Unannounced** checks may be justified when there are signs that practice changes once a check is announced. They need the sponsor's approval and clear rules for access.
Auditor time cost = number of auditors × days × cost per auditor-day. Example: 2 auditors for 3 days at J$30,000 per auditor-day = 2 × 3 × 30,000 = J$180,000. Add report writing and follow-up time.

A checklist turns each criterion into a question that can be answered 'yes', 'no' or 'not applicable' with evidence. It makes sure that **every requirement is checked in the same way** and nothing is forgotten. A checklist is a guide, not a limit: if the auditor sees a danger or a breach that is not listed (for example a blocked exit), she should raise it with the manager at once and record it.

head: Criterion
Checklist question
Evidence
rows: Does each extinguisher have a service tag dated within 12 months?
Is the box complete against the list and checked monthly?
Is the book completed with time in and out for the sample days?
Are staff files in a locked cabinet with access limited?

blocks.p: The opening meeting, held at the start with the auditee's manager and staff, **confirms the plan, timetable and ground rules**: scope, who will be interviewed, access, health and safety, confidentiality, when the closing meeting will be.

head: Source
What it is
Strength
Weakness
rows: Logs, certificates, permits, receipts, training files, minutes
Can be wrong, missing, or filled in afterwards
Only shows one moment; people may behave differently when watched
Opinions; may be incomplete or defensive
Checking a temperature, a count or a calibration

blocks.p: Use the sources **together**: what a person says is checked against records, and records are checked against what you see. **Objective evidence** is information that can be verified, for example signed temperature logs for the past month. A supervisor's statement that all forklift drivers are trained must be confirmed by the training records of a sample of drivers.

blocks.note: Practice may differ from procedure. Watch a task being done, as well as reading the procedure for it.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: An auditor cannot check every record, so she checks a **sample**. A sample should be:

ul: **random** or chosen by a set method, so that every record has an equal chance of being picked. The auditee should not choose the sample, because it could be chosen to hide problems;
**big enough** for the risk: higher risk needs a larger sample;
**spread** over the whole period and all sites or shifts in the scope.

blocks.p: Sample size from a percentage: 5% of 1,200 payslips = 1,200 × 0.05 = 60 payslips. If a sample shows many failures, widen it.

ul: Explain the purpose and that the interview is about the process, not the person.
Ask **open questions** ('Show me how you check the cold room'), listen calmly, and avoid leading questions.
Do not argue or show disapproval.
Check what you hear against records and observation.
Interview a mix of managers and the staff who do the work.

blocks.p: Choose what to watch and where, rather than letting the auditee choose the areas to show you. Watch work at different times if the scope allows. Record what you saw, where and when.

**Working papers** are the auditor's own record: the checklist with answers, notes, sample lists, photographs, copies of key records and interview notes. They must allow each finding to be **traced back to its evidence**, and another person to follow what was done. Record dates, names (or job titles), references to documents, sample sizes and results. Keep them secure and confidential.

ul: Be polite and punctual; do not interrupt work more than needed.
Respect confidentiality: keep medical, pay and other personal details private and record only what the audit needs.
Do not accept gifts or hospitality. **Decline politely and report the offer**.
Stay within the scope. If asked to add areas, agree it with the audit sponsor and amend the plan, or schedule a separate audit.

If you find something dangerous or illegal that needs urgent action (for example a serious accident that may not have been reported as the law requires), raise it **urgently with senior management**, and do not wait for the report.

head: Grade
Meaning
Example
rows: The requirement is met, with evidence
Signed temperature logs complete for the month
An isolated or small failure; no serious risk; the system generally works
1 of 30 staff files lacks a signed form; the other 29 are complete
A serious, widespread or repeated failure; a legal or licence breach; a failure of the whole system; or a significant risk to people
No trained first aider on any shift for a year, although the licence and policy require one
The requirement is met, but could be met better
Extinguisher tags are valid but the register is hard to read

blocks.p: Grade by **evidence and criteria**, not by who is involved. A good test: how serious is the risk, how widespread is the failure, and does it breach a legal requirement or licence condition? Be consistent from audit to audit.
**Compliance rate = items that comply ÷ items checked × 100.**

head: Example
Working
Rate
rows: Of a hotel's 80 food handlers, 76 hold current permits

blocks.p: A rate is information, not a verdict. A rate of 95% may still conceal a major finding if the 5% that fail are the safety-critical items. Always look at what failed.

A finding names **what** is wrong. A corrective action must remove **why** it happened (the **root cause**). A useful technique is the **five whys**: keep asking 'why?' until you reach a cause that management can fix.

head: Why?
Answer
rows: Why were the daily van checks missed?
Drivers did not complete the sheet
Sheets were kept in the office, not in the van
No holder was fitted in the vans
The sheet was never added to the new-vehicle set-up routine
No process to equip new vehicles with the check sheet

blocks.p: Other tools: a cause-and-effect (fishbone) diagram, and asking the staff concerned.

blocks.h: Correction, corrective action and preventive action

head: Term
Meaning
Example
rows: Fixes the specific problem found now
Removing out-of-date items from a shelf
Removes the root cause so that it does not happen again
Fixing the stock-rotation system and training
Stops a similar problem occurring elsewhere
Applying the new rotation system to all stores

blocks.p: A good finding states the **criterion**, the **condition found** with numbers, and the **evidence**: 'Procedure CR-4 requires extinguishers to be serviced yearly. Two of eight extinguishers checked on the first floor had no service tag dated this year (working paper 12).' It is factual, specific and free of opinion or blame.

blocks.note: Avoid words such as 'careless', 'lazy' or 'always'. Say what you saw and counted.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Closing meeting and the audit report

blocks.p: At the end of the audit, the auditor presents the findings to the auditee's manager, to confirm that they are understood and accurate.

flow: Thank the team and recall the scope
Present good practice and compliance rates
Present each finding with its evidence and grade
Review disputed findings with the evidence and note any disagreement
Agree the date for the corrective action plan and the follow-up
Confirm when the report will be issued

blocks.p: If the auditee's manager **disagrees** with a finding, stay calm, show the evidence, listen and check new information. If new evidence changes the facts, change the finding. If not, keep the finding and **record the disagreement** in the report; do not argue or trade a finding for a favour. An offer of an explanation (for example a broken thermometer) helps find the root cause but does not remove the finding. If the manager threatens to complain to a senior manager, explain that he has a right to raise it through the sponsor, and that the evidence stands.

head: Part
Content
rows: Audit title, dates, auditors, auditee, sponsor
The main results and the overall conclusion, in a few lines
What was audited and against what
Each finding with criterion, evidence, grade and a reference to working papers; compliance rates
What must be done, and opportunities for improvement
Corrective action plan (or reference to it)

blocks.p: The final report normally goes to **the audited area's manager and the audit sponsor**. It is marked confidential, kept securely and shared only with those who need it. Do not include unneeded personal data, and describe people by job title, not name, where possible.
For each finding the auditee prepares, and the auditor reviews, a plan that includes:

ul: the finding and its grade;
the root cause;
the corrective action (and any immediate correction);
the person responsible (one owner);
the due date (earlier for major findings);
how completion will be checked (the evidence to be shown).

head: Finding
Root cause
Action
Owner
Due
Evidence of completion
rows: Fit holders; train drivers; supervisor weekly check
Add services to the maintenance calendar

blocks.p: The auditee reports that actions are complete. The auditor then **verifies with evidence that each action works**: for example, by sampling the new records or observing the new process. An action that is done but does not stop the problem is not complete.

flow: Auditee completes the action and reports
Auditor checks the evidence and samples new results
Action is closed if it works; otherwise it is reopened
Overdue actions are reported to the sponsor
Results go into the audit programme and the register

blocks.p: Track the **percentage of actions closed on time** and the **overdue** ones. Overdue % = overdue actions ÷ actions due × 100 (for example, 3 of 20 = 15%). If an owner says that he has no budget or authority, the compliance manager should **escalate to senior management or the audit committee**, who must either provide resources or formally accept the risk and reset the date. A repeated failure to act, especially where a legal breach is involved, must be escalated.

blocks.h: Keeping a business compliant between audits

ul: A **compliance calendar** showing renewals, reports and checks, with an owner for each.
Regular **self-checks** by area managers using short checklists.
Training so that staff know the rules that apply to them.
A simple way for staff to report concerns.
Management review of audit results, trends and repeat findings.

blocks.h: Judging whether the audit programme works

head: Measure
What it shows
rows: Number and grade of findings over time
Whether the audits find the right risks

blocks.p: If repeat findings rise, the actions are treating symptoms, not root causes.

blocks.h: Typical requirements audited in Jamaican workplaces

head: Area
What a compliance audit might check (by purpose)
rows: Food handlers hold current permits; premises and equipment meet sanitation rules; temperature and cleaning logs are kept
Certificate current; extinguishers serviced; exits clear; drills held; first aid supplies; accident reporting
Written terms; leave and records; correct pay; statutory deductions remitted on time
General Consumption Tax (GCT) charged and shown on invoices as required; returns filed on time
Personal data collected lawfully, used for stated purposes, kept secure, kept no longer than needed, disposed of safely, with consent where required
Operating, trade and environmental permits current and conditions met
Waste, chemicals and emissions managed as permits require

blocks.p: An audit that finds personal data **kept long after the business needs it** most likely breaches the data protection law on keeping data. The auditor describes the law by its purpose and refers questions to the legal adviser. Do not quote sections or penalties unless the law has been checked.
A hotel group that must keep its operating licence should have its internal audit check the licence conditions **before the regulator's inspection**, so that gaps are found and fixed first.

head: Issue
What to do
rows: Do not audit your own work or an area where you have an interest; declare conflicts
Base findings on evidence; do not change a finding to please or to punish
Keep personal and commercial information private; store working papers securely; share only with those entitled
Decline politely and report the offer
Study the relevant laws and standards before the audit, so that you can judge fairly whether practice meets them
Raise a possible legal breach or danger urgently with senior management

blocks.note: When auditing records that contain personal data, record only what the audit needs. If you see medical details or pay data, keep them private.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: explain compliance, a compliance audit, the register of obligations and the types of audit.
state the principles of auditing, including independence, objectivity and confidentiality.
build a risk-based programme using likelihood × impact.
write the objectives, scope and criteria and an audit plan.
prepare a checklist and a sampling method, and work out a sample size.
run an opening meeting and gather evidence from records, observation and interviews.
keep working papers that trace each finding to its evidence.
grade findings as major, minor or an opportunity for improvement and work out a compliance rate.
use the five whys to reach the root cause, and tell correction from corrective action.
hold a closing meeting and handle a disputed finding.
write a factual audit report and send it to the right people.
prepare a corrective action plan, verify actions, track overdue actions and escalate when needed.
explain how to keep a business compliant between audits and how to judge the audit programme.

terms: Meeting the laws, licences, standards and policies that apply.
The requirements practice is measured against.
The areas, activities and period an audit covers.
The list of obligations with owners, evidence and dates.
The auditor's record of evidence and checks.
A sample in which every record has an equal chance of selection.
A failure to meet a requirement.
A serious, widespread or repeated failure, or a breach of a legal or licence requirement.
A suggestion where the rule is met but could be met better.
The underlying reason a problem occurred.
Asking 'why?' repeatedly to reach the root cause.
The actions, owners and dates to fix findings.
The meeting where findings are presented to the auditee.
No personal interest in or responsibility for the area audited.

c1.title: A paint and chemicals distributor plans its audits
c1.text: Camille Brown is the compliance manager of a paint and chemicals distributor in Kingston. She has listed the company's obligations and scored three areas for the coming year: chemical storage and the environmental permit (likelihood 3, impact 5), customer personal data (likelihood 4, impact 3) and licence and permit renewals (likelihood 2, impact 4). Time allows only two audits this year. She will begin with an audit of chemical storage at the Kingston warehouse.

c2.title: An audit at a private school in Montego Bay
c2.text: A trained internal auditor visits a private school in Montego Bay to audit fire safety, school bus records and the security of student files. The principal says the school holds a fire drill every term and offers to walk the auditor round 'the best classrooms'. The drill log shows only two drills last year. The student files cabinet is unlocked. Part-way through, the principal asks the auditor also to check the canteen, which is not in the audit plan.

c3.title: An audit of statutory payments at a supermarket chain
c3.text: An auditor checks how a supermarket chain pays its statutory payroll deductions to the authorities. The payroll team produced 1,200 payslips last year. The auditor samples 5% of them at random and checks 48 monthly remittance records. Of the 48 records, 42 were paid on time and 6 were paid late, all of them in the months when the senior finance officer who signs the payments was travelling. The same lateness was reported in the previous audit.

c4.title: A cold-room finding at a fish processing plant
c4.text: At a fish processing plant in Old Harbour, the procedure requires the cold-room temperature to be recorded every 6 hours, which is 4 readings a day. An audit of the last 40 days found 8 readings missing. At the closing meeting the plant manager, Mr Nelson, says the gaps happened because the thermometer was broken for three days and offers a repair invoice. He says he will complain to the general manager if the finding is kept.

c5.title: A customer-data audit at a retail chain
c5.text: Michelle Walker is an internal auditor at a retail chain. She has been asked to audit how the chain handles customers' personal data collected on loyalty-card forms. Her brother-in-law owns the firm that shreds the chain's old paper records. While visiting a store, she finds a box of old loyalty-card forms in an open skip behind the shop. She will keep working papers on her laptop and then write a confidential report.

questions.q: Camille adds each obligation to her compliance register. What should each entry include?
o: The name of the auditor who will check it and the date of the last audit only
A copy of the full law, and nothing about who is responsible for it
The requirement and its source, an owner, the evidence and the renewal date
The cost of the penalty if the requirement is not met, and the date of the last fine
questions.why: A useful register tells who owns each requirement, where it comes from, what evidence proves compliance and when it must be renewed or reported. This links obligations to audit criteria.

questions.q: Time allows only two audits. Which should Camille choose, and why?
o: Chemical storage and customer data, the two highest scores
Licence renewals and customer data, because they are the easiest to audit
Chemical storage and licence renewals, because they have the highest impact scores
Whichever two the managers volunteer for, so that they will cooperate with it
questions.why: Likelihood × impact gives 15 for chemical storage, 12 for personal data and 8 for licences. A risk-based programme audits the highest scores first.

questions.q: The warehouse manager asks to approve the audit criteria himself before the audit starts. How should Camille respond?
o: Let him choose the criteria, since he knows the warehouse best of all
Refuse to show him the plan until the audit has been completed
Agree, but only for the parts of the permit that he finds hard to meet
Share the plan and hear his comments, but the criteria come from the rules
questions.why: The criteria come from the law, the permit and the company's procedures, not from the auditee. He may comment on the plan, but the sponsor approves it, so the audit stays independent and objective.

questions.q: Which set of criteria is most suitable for the chemical-storage audit?
o: The auditor's own view of what good practice ought to look like
The permit conditions, the law, company procedures and safety data sheets
The practice at the best-run competitor, whatever the law may require
Last year's audit report only, since it has already been agreed by all
questions.why: Criteria are the rules practice is checked against: the law, permit conditions, the organisation's own procedures and technical sheets. They must be agreed in advance, not chosen by the auditor's own taste.

questions.q: The principal says the school holds a fire drill every term, but the log shows only two last year. What should the auditor do?
o: Accept the principal's word, since she is responsible for the whole school
Rely on the log, record the difference and ask her to explain
Record that three drills were held, since the policy says that they should be
Tell the teachers that the principal has been untruthful about the drills
questions.why: Records and observation are more reliable than a spoken statement. The auditor records what the evidence shows and asks for an explanation, without accusing anyone.

questions.q: The principal offers to walk the auditor round the best classrooms. What is the best response?
o: Accept, since the principal knows the school and its rooms best
Accept, and also check the staff-room, so that the visit is fair
Decline, and cancel the observation part of the audit completely
Thank her, but choose the rooms by the auditor's own sampling
questions.why: If the auditee chooses what is seen, problems may be hidden. The auditor should select the sample by a set method, politely.

questions.q: The student files cabinet is unlocked. Which requirement is the most relevant criterion?
o: The data protection law's rule that personal data be kept secure
The law on keeping school fees records for a number of years
The fire certificate conditions for the school premises
The school bus fitness rules and the conditions of its licence
questions.why: Student records are personal data. An unlocked cabinet is a question of security, which the data protection law, by its purpose, requires.

questions.q: The principal asks the auditor to add the canteen to the audit. What should the auditor do?
o: Add it at once, since the principal herself has asked for it
Refuse, and say nothing more to the principal about the canteen
Agree it with the sponsor and amend the plan, or audit it separately
Check the canteen quickly and include it with no plan or criteria
questions.why: Scope is set in the plan agreed with the sponsor. Changes should be authorised and recorded, or handled as a separate audit with its own criteria.

questions.q: The auditor samples 5% of the 1,200 payslips. How many payslips is this?
questions.why: 1,200 × 5% = 60 payslips.

questions.q: Of 48 remittance records, 42 were paid on time. What is the compliance rate?
questions.why: 42 ÷ 48 × 100 = 87.5%. The 6 late payments make up 12.5%.

questions.q: The same lateness was found last year and carries a legal penalty. How should it be graded?
o: As a minor non-conformity, because most of the payments were on time
As an opportunity for improvement, because the money was paid in the end
As compliant, because the amounts paid were correct each month
As a major non-conformity, because it is a repeated legal failure
questions.why: A repeated failure to meet a legal requirement shows that the system does not work, which makes it major. A good overall rate does not remove a repeated legal breach.

questions.q: Asking 'why?' repeatedly, the auditor finds that payments are late because only one officer can sign. Which corrective action best addresses the root cause?
o: Warn the senior finance officer to travel less in the year ahead
Appoint a deputy signatory and put due dates on a compliance calendar
Pay the penalties from a central fund each year as they arise
Move the due dates in the compliance register to suit the signatory
questions.why: The root cause is that the process depends on one person. A deputy signatory and a calendar remove that weakness; warnings or paying penalties treat the symptoms.

questions.q: Mr Nelson offers a repair invoice for the thermometer. How should the auditor treat this?
o: Drop the finding, since the invoice explains the gaps in the readings
Check it and note his point, but keep the finding
Ignore the invoice, since the closing meeting is not the place for evidence
Lower the grade of every finding at the plant to be fair to him
questions.why: An explanation helps find the root cause, and new evidence should be checked, but the readings were still not recorded as the procedure required. The finding stays, with his explanation noted.

questions.q: There should have been 160 readings in 40 days, and 8 were missing. What percentage was recorded?
questions.why: 152 of 160 were recorded: 152 ÷ 160 × 100 = 95%. Missing readings were 5%.

questions.q: Mr Nelson says he will complain to the general manager. What is the best response?
o: Say he may raise it through the sponsor, and the evidence stands
Withdraw the finding to avoid trouble with the general manager
Warn him that complaining will make the final report worse for him
Agree to leave the finding out of the written report altogether
questions.why: An auditee may use the proper route to raise a concern, but findings must rest on evidence and cannot be bargained away or threatened.

questions.q: The plant says the broken thermometer will be repaired. Which is a corrective action rather than a correction?
o: Replacing the broken thermometer with a new one at once today
Recording the missing readings as 'not available' in the cold-room log
A calibration routine, a spare thermometer and daily supervisor checks
Repairing the broken thermometer within the course of the week
questions.why: Replacing the thermometer fixes the immediate problem (a correction). A corrective action changes the system so that missing readings do not happen again.

questions.q: Michelle's brother-in-law owns the shredding firm. What should she do about auditing disposal of records?
o: Audit it normally and mention the connection to the sponsor afterwards
Avoid the question of disposal in her report to keep matters simple
Declare the connection and ask that another auditor cover that part
Ask her brother-in-law for his own records of what was shredded
questions.why: Independence means no personal interest in the area audited. A declared connection should lead to another auditor taking that part, so that the finding cannot be questioned.

questions.q: Where should Michelle keep working papers that contain customers' data?
o: On a secure, password-protected device, kept only as long as policy allows
On her personal email account, so that she can reach them from home
In a shared folder open to every member of the team and the managers
On paper in the boot of her car until the final report has been issued
questions.why: Working papers contain personal data and must be kept secure and confidential, and only as long as needed. Open or personal storage risks a breach.

questions.q: In checking the loyalty-card forms, what should Michelle check about consent?
o: That the forms were printed in the company's colours and its logo
That the forms contain as many personal details as it is possible to take
That all the forms are filed in the order of the customers' dates of birth
That customers were told how their data would be used, and agreed
questions.why: The data protection law, by its purpose, expects personal data to be collected for a stated purpose with the person's knowledge and, where required, consent. The auditor checks these points against the forms and processes.

questions.q: What should Michelle do about the box of forms in the open skip?
o: Take the forms home for safekeeping and say nothing to anyone else
Tell the store manager and senior management at once, and record it
Wait until the end of the audit before telling anyone about the forms
Ask a staff member to burn the forms that same afternoon after closing
questions.why: Unsecured disposal exposes customers' data and needs urgent action. The auditor raises it immediately so it can be secured and records the facts, but does not handle or destroy the forms without authority.
